title: It works on my machine
summary: Why containers exist, what an image is, and how image names point into registries.

steps.title: It works on my machine
body: An application is never just its code. To run, it needs a **runtime** (the .NET runtime, Node 22, Python 3.13), **system libraries** (OpenSSL, ICU, libc), **files** in the right places and **configuration**.
Every machine it lands on (your laptop, a teammate's Mac, the CI runner, the production server) has a slightly different set of those. That is where "it works on my machine" comes from.
A **container** fixes this by shipping the application *together with everything it needs* as one sealed package, and running that package in an isolated box on any machine with a container engine.
```text
without containers                 with containers
│ your code   │  + hope the        │ your code               │
└─────────────┘    server has      │ .NET 10 runtime         │
.NET 10, ICU,   │ ICU, OpenSSL, libc      │  one image,
the right       │ config defaults         │  runs the same
Docker is the tool that popularised this. It builds the package, stores it, and runs it.

steps.prompt: A team's API runs fine on the developer's laptop but crashes on the server with `libicu not found`. What is the container answer to this?
options: Ship the API as an image that already contains the ICU library and the runtime it was tested with
Install ICU on the server and write the steps in a wiki page
Compile the API in Release mode so it no longer needs ICU
Run the API as administrator on the server
steps.explain: The image carries its own dependencies, so the server only needs a container engine. Wiki steps drift; that is exactly the problem containers remove.

steps.title: Images and containers
body: Two words you will use all day:
- An **image** is a read-only package: a filesystem (your app plus its runtime and libraries) and some metadata, such as which command to run. It never changes once built.
- A **container** is a running (or stopped) **instance** of an image. Docker gives it a thin writable layer on top, its own process tree, its own network interface and its own hostname.
```text
image  api:1.4  (read-only)
container    container    container      three instances,
api-1        api-2        api-3          each with its own writable layer
If you know C#: an image is like a **class**, a container is like an **object** created from it. You can start many containers from one image, and deleting a container never changes the image.

steps.prompt: Is each statement about an **image** or a **container**?
items: Has a process running inside it
Is pushed to and pulled from a registry
Has its own writable layer that disappears when it is removed
steps.explain: Images are the packaged, immutable artifact you build, tag and share. Containers are the live things that run, write files and show up in `docker ps`.

steps.title: Registries and image names
body: Images are stored and shared in a **registry**: Docker Hub (`docker.io`), GitHub (`ghcr.io`), Microsoft (`mcr.microsoft.com`), or your company's own (Azure Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Harbor).
A full image reference has up to four parts:
```text
mcr.microsoft.com / dotnet/aspnet : 10.0
└──── registry ──┘ └ repository ┘ └tag┘
Docker fills in what you leave out:
- No registry? It means **`docker.io`** (Docker Hub).
- A Docker Hub name with no slash, like `nginx`, is an *official image* and lives under **`library/`**.
- No tag? It means **`latest`**, which is just a tag name, not a promise of "newest".

So `docker pull nginx` pulls `docker.io/library/nginx:latest`. A first segment counts as a registry only if it contains a `.` or a `:` or is `localhost`; otherwise `myteam/api` is a Docker Hub repository.

steps.prompt: Match each short reference to the full name Docker uses.
steps.explain: Defaults: registry `docker.io`, namespace `library/` for official images, tag `latest`. `localhost:5000` is a registry because it contains a `:`.

steps.prompt: You type this. What full image reference does Docker actually pull? Type it exactly.
steps.explain: No registry means Docker Hub, an official image means `library/`, and no tag means `latest`. In real projects pin a version tag such as `postgres:17` so every machine gets the same thing.

steps.prompt: Why is relying on `:latest` in production a bad idea?
options: `latest` is just a tag that moves whenever someone pushes; two machines pulling it a week apart can get different images
Docker refuses to run `latest` images in detached mode
`latest` images cannot be pulled from private registries
steps.explain: Pin a specific tag (`api:1.4.2`) or even an immutable digest (`api@sha256:...`) so a deploy is repeatable.

steps.prompt: Complete the command that downloads version 10.0 of the ASP.NET Core runtime image from Microsoft's registry.
steps.explain: `docker pull` downloads; the registry goes first, then the repository, then `:tag`.

steps.title: Name and tag images on a real Engine
prompt: This terminal is your own machine with a **real Docker Engine** inside it (no network, so nothing can be pulled; the
images you need are already there). Look first: `docker image ls`.
1. Your team pushes to `registry.example.com`. Give the local `alpine:3.24` image a second name,
2. Write the **full** reference Docker really means by `busybox:1.37` (registry, repository and tag) into
3. `shop/old:latest` is a stale name. Remove that **name** only: `busybox:1.37` must still be there afterwards.

checks.name: registry.example.com/shop/base:3.24 is the same image as alpine:3.24
checks.cmd: test "$(docker image inspect -f '{{.Id}}' registry.example.com/shop/base:3.24)" = "$(docker image inspect -f '{{.Id}}' alpine:3.24)"
checks.fail: There is no `registry.example.com/shop/base:3.24` pointing at the alpine image yet. `docker tag SOURCE TARGET` adds a name.

checks.name: busybox.txt has the fully qualified reference
checks.fail: Not quite. A name without a registry goes to Docker Hub (`docker.io`), and an official image without a namespace lives under `library/`.

checks.name: shop/old:latest is gone, busybox:1.37 is still there
checks.cmd: ! docker image inspect shop/old:latest >/dev/null 2>&1 && docker image inspect busybox:1.37 >/dev/null
checks.fail: `shop/old:latest` should be gone while `busybox:1.37` stays. `docker rmi NAME` on one of several names only removes that name ("Untagged").

hints: `docker tag` takes the existing name first, then the new one.
The full form is `registry/namespace/repository:tag`. Docker Hub is `docker.io`, official images are in `library`.
`docker rmi shop/old:latest` prints `Untagged:` and keeps the image, because `busybox:1.37` still names it.
steps.explain: A tag is only a name pointing at an image ID: `docker tag` added one in an instant, and `docker rmi` on one of two names only untagged it. The registry part of a name is where `docker push` would send it, which is why teams tag images with their registry's host name before pushing.
